questions.subject: ACCOUNTING
questions.stem: Case 9001: Westbrook Company has fixed costs of $4,700 and a contribution margin ratio of 40 percent. What sales level is required to break even?

options.misconception: treats fixed costs as the break-even sales amount
multiplies fixed costs by the margin ratio rather than dividing
uses the complement of the contribution margin ratio

questions.explanation: Break-even sales in dollars equal fixed costs divided by the contribution margin ratio, so $4,700 over forty percent gives $11,750. Multiplying by the ratio or using its complement would not identify the sales that cover all costs.
questions.hint: Divide fixed costs by the contribution margin ratio.

questions.subject: ACCOUNTING
questions.stem: Case 9002: For Westbrook Works, sales are $4,350, variable costs are $1,550, and fixed costs are $350. What is operating income?

options.misconception: stops at contribution margin and ignores fixed costs
ignores variable costs in the income calculation
adds fixed costs instead of deducting them

questions.explanation: Operating income is contribution margin less fixed costs, so starting from sales of $4,350, subtract $1,550 of variable costs and $350 of fixed costs to get $2,450. Stopping at contribution margin would leave fixed costs unpaid.
questions.hint: Subtract both variable and fixed costs from sales.

questions.subject: ACCOUNTING
questions.stem: Case 9004: Ashford Traders can make a component for $3,650 variable cost per batch or buy it for $14,550 per batch, and no fixed costs would change. What is the advantage of making rather than buying per batch? A positive figure favors making.

options.misconception: reverses the sign of the incremental advantage
adds the two alternatives instead of comparing them
reports only the purchase price as the advantage

questions.explanation: When fixed costs are unchanged, the relevant comparison is the avoidable variable cost of making, $3,650, versus the purchase price of $14,550, giving an advantage of $10,900 per batch for making. Adding the options or reversing the order ignores the logic of incremental analysis.
